title: Pink Elephant hosts 4th Annual Route 66 UFO Festival
content:
An alien statue stands outside a silver saucer at the Pink Elephant. (Bruce Darnell photo)

By Bruce Darnell • Coming around for a fourth encounter, the Pink Elephant in Livingston brought back the aliens for its fall festival, which ran from Aug. 29 to Aug. 30.

Bigger than last year in scale, with more vendor stands and multiple new events, the festival ended up with a lower attendance, which is believed to have been caused by high temperatures, Marketing and Event Coordinator Suzann Hormell said.

“We went down from three days to two because of the heat,” Hormell said. “But we had 50 vendors, the intergalactic pinup contest was a huge success and we had four different speakers.”

Heat was an issue in planning the event last year, as Pink Elephant co-owner Wayne Pickerill said the timing of the event depends entirely on the weather. This year, weekend temperatures peaked between 84 and 86 degrees.

But some of the planned events accounted for the heat, like the splash parade.

“The splash parade is aliens versus humanity,” Hormell said. “It’s a water gun fight, where the aliens in the parade fight the people watching. We’re using water guns, buckets and jets … It starts in the middle of town and drives out here.”

Hormell said the parade was a charity to donate canned goods to the Livingston Park Association. Entry into the parade cost five canned goods per person. Another charity event was the Alien Run 5K, which collected funds for a food pantry in the Mount Olive Library.

Another charity event was the second intergalactic pinup contest, hosted by the Midwest Pinup Charity Mingle. Hormell said funds are donated to a charity of the group’s choice, which this year is a charity for suicide hotlines.

Besides the events, the market vendors had a plethora of items to pick from. Some were alien-related while others were crafts that can be found at any typical festival.

Like previous years, the festival had a set of bouncy castles for children. New to this year were $10 horse rides provided by Massa Stables LLC and access inside the Pink Elephant’s metallic UFO.

The UFO was intended to provide a space for presentations but cryptid investigator and event speaker David Eller said the UFO was hard for people to enter and exit.

Eller was present with Janice, his wife and collaborator. The pair specialize in bigfoot hunting, having been researchers for 30 and 15 years respectively but had a few encounters with UFOs they planned to discuss that often intersect with their specialization. 

He remembers reports he heard of a hairy giant being dropped from a UFO, though said events like that are hard to investigate since it could have happened anywhere. Janice remembers her youth in Alabama staring at starlit skies and seeing lights dash around in impossible ways. 

Another speaker named Harold Benny said the hunt for bigfoot was like an always moving set of needles in haystacks. All three had spent large amounts of time in the woods at dark, hearing unexplained creaks and cracks throughout the trees, oftentimes when they weren’t recording. So they always bring with them an array of technology to try and document the elusive, hairy beast.

Three of the event’s four speakers pose for a photo. From left: Harold Benny, Janice Eller, and David Eller. (Bruce Darnell photo)

“People have to understand that the monsters of their childhood are real and dangerous,” David said. “For me, that’s part of the appeal … but you can’t just go off of what we say. You’ve got to have your own experiences — get out there in the woods and live life. That’s what it’s all about.”

Hormell said the Pink Elephant’s next big events are the Haunted Hundred on Oct. 10 and 11, which is part of the 100 year celebration of Route 66. Their next cryptid event, the Bigfoot Festival, is usually annually hosted on Mother’s Day weekend.

Three intergalactic pin-up winners pose after the contest. From left: Lady Justice/Shonda L. Justice, third place; Miss Sweet as Sugar Sarah/Sarah Carine, second place; and Kitty Von Kisses/Erin McRoy, first place. (Bruce Darnell photo)
